inserts.title: Zero crossings mark timing inside the mixture
paragraphs: A zero crossing is the moment when the electrical voltage changes sign, and it gives a reproducible timing landmark on each carrier cycle. Amplitude and zero-crossing timing are two different properties of the same mixed waveform. Neither sensory pathway directly receives an isolated copy of the neighbor's signal, so both cues come from one summed input.

The illustrated carrier runs at 500 Hz, so each cycle lasts 2 ms. A timing shift in the landmark occupies a small part of that cycle, which is why the fish must resolve fine differences inside a repeating waveform. Heiligenberg's oscilloscope record keeps the slow envelope and the fast carrier on one trace, so both features appear together.

Sorting these cues requires reading each timing landmark against the amplitude change at the same point in the cycle. Because the nervous system receives both properties through one channel, each measure must be interpreted in the context of the other. A beat rate alone carries no sign information, so the timing evidence must supply it.
notes: Zero crossings mark timing inside the mixture.

inserts.title: Regional stimulation holds one cue constant
paragraphs: A natural neighbor changes several cues together, whereas regional stimulation can vary one cue while another stays fixed. That control let the investigator treat the timing offset between two regions as a separate variable. The published stimulus tested the relative timing cue on its own, apart from the beat rate. The offset behaves as a second variable beside the modulation.

Heiligenberg's stimulators were controlled electronically, so each region's modulation could be repeated across trials. Exchanging the region assignments moved the phase modulation to the other region, with the amplitude schedule fixed. The constant phase offset between regions was held fixed during each exchange. At near-zero offset, timing of the normal kind yielded a negative shift for positive Δf.

Relative timing defines the exchange, and the stimulus isolates that variable from the amplitude schedule. The same experiments also showed that the offset between regions shapes the size of the response, not only its direction. The behavioral reversal shows which cue controls the response, and it points to the neural site of the computation as the next layer to map.
notes: Regional stimulation holds one cue constant.

inserts.title: Electronic controls mimic the spike's rising edge
paragraphs: The electronic controls were adjusted to resemble the steep rising portion of a neural spike, because a different spike shape could change threshold-crossing precision. Intracellular recordings also reduced contamination from small extracellular signals, which helped distinguish biological variability from the recording method. Those controls kept the spike shape constant across trials. The rising edge sets the threshold timing.

A single afferent's spike train is one sample of the timing signal, which is why the authors pointed to parallel inputs. The spike mimics passed through the same equipment, so instrument uncertainty was measured on the same timescale as the afferent data. The spike mimics directly tested the recording system. Its spread stayed narrow.

Afferent timing alone leaves the behavioral precision within the 300-ms response latency poorly. Pooling across many inputs fits both the afferent spread and the behavioral result, because each additional afferent adds a partly independent timing estimate. The 300-ms response latency gives the nervous system time to pool many stimulus cycles before the fish responds. The timing estimates stay partly independent.
notes: Electronic controls mimic the spike's rising edge.

inserts.title: Afferent and spherical cells occupy different sites
paragraphs: The primary afferent's cell body lies in a peripheral ganglion, whereas the spherical cell is a central neuron in the ELL. These are successive elements of one pathway, not different names for the same cell. The transition from a peripheral to a central cell body marks the point where the signal enters the brain. The circuit begins at the receptor.

The parallel P-type pathway carries amplitude information and projects to different central targets than the T-type route. Routing the two pathways to different targets allows the torus to receive both cue types through separate channels. Routing timing through the ELL keeps phase information separate from amplitude information until the torus. Phase information stays separate there.

Spherical-cell axons reach lamina VI, where giant cells receive the locked timing. Each stage carries the phase of the original carrier to the next, which allows the torus to compare arrival times across regions. The giant cells in lamina VI receive timing from spherical cells rather than from the periphery. Phase locking is conserved across this step.
notes: Afferent and spherical cells occupy different sites.

inserts.title: Junction recordings tied to labeled contacts
paragraphs: Carr and colleagues linked electrophysiology to an identifiable contact by recording near a terminal and labeling the same pathway. Electrical transmission was not inferred from the mere proximity of unlabeled cells, so each recorded event is tied to a specific anatomical contact. The labeled terminals were identified in the same preparation as the recordings. The contact was labeled in every panel.

The accompanying micrograph carries a 20-µm scale bar, which sets the size reference for the contact. At that scale the terminal recordings resolve individual contacts rather than whole cell populations. A junction recorded at this resolution can be attributed to one identified contact. Spikes recorded there carry the timing of the presynaptic side. Recording and labeling were combined.

Spikes and potentials that cross the junction in reverse differ from newly generated sensory events, since they originate in the giant cell. Events of this kind are what an electrical synapse would produce when current flows in both directions. Gap junctions are the structural basis for that electrical coupling. Their contacts can carry current in either direction.
notes: Junction recordings tied to labeled contacts.

The laminae define functional depth rather than separate behaviors.

That projection reaches a structure outside the toral laminae, so it is not one of the lamina-specific streams described above. Its position is separate.

Amplitude and phase inputs converge within deeper toral layers, where the combination-sensitive neurons of later experiments were recorded. Those deeper neurons receive the streams that enter the upper laminae, so the layered arrangement sets the order of processing. Their arrangement determines which cells receive the timing signal first. Each stream reaches the deeper laminae in order.

inserts.title: Sensitivity to instant timing differs from change
paragraphs: The two kinds of test distinguish sensitivity to instantaneous timing from sensitivity to temporal change. A held phase value probes the steady response, while a rapid sweep probes the response during changing input. Each test reveals a different feature of the same comparator. A held phase value tests stationary timing, which a sweep alone leaves hidden.

In the 2-Hz tests the two regional signals moved together, so only their relative timing changed. Losing the head carrier widened the range of the cycle over which the cell fired, so the response depends on carrier presence. Head carrier removal changed the activity pattern across the whole cycle. The timing relation changed with the carrier.

A neuron that responds to instantaneous phase is not identical to one that responds to changing phase, so one cell can carry both kinds of information. Sustained offsets held the phase constant long enough to measure a steady firing level, which a rapid scan lacks. Its response state depends on the carrier present in the reference region.
notes: Sensitivity to instant timing differs from change.

inserts.title: The E-type label refers to response, not transmitter
paragraphs: The label excitatory in E-type refers to excitation during amplitude increase, not to the transmitter the cell releases. An I-type sensory preference likewise says nothing about whether the neuron inhibits its postsynaptic targets. Each label describes a response in the torus, and no label describes a transmitter. The four-class scheme is built from sensory response properties alone.

The published summary includes pure amplitude coders, phase coders, and cells sensitive to both variables. These stages are experimentally distinguishable, so the population contains each kind of representation. The published summary identifies these stages by their recorded responses. Pure amplitude coders respond to one variable, whereas dual-sensitive cells respond to both. The stages are defined by their responses.

Physiological response class and synaptic transmitter identity are separate properties of a neuron. Reading a response class as a transmitter identity would conflate two different properties. The labeled morphology in deeper laminae supplies an anatomical correlate for each class. Each class needs its own morphological and physiological test. The identity of the transmitter is a separate question.

inserts.title: The older single-population account
paragraphs: The older account treated decreases as a weakening of the same neurons that drive increases. Selective lesions supported a different organization, in which each route alters one direction of frequency change while the other direction stays available. The lesion data required two routes, each acting on one direction of frequency change. Each route acts on one direction only.

Selective lesions of one route left the other direction available, so each direction of frequency change can be lost independently. The two directions have separable anatomical bases in the prepacemaker region. Each route reaches a distinct prepacemaker station, the dorsal route through PPn-G and the ventral route through SPPn. The stations were tested with lesions, stimulation, and pharmacology.

The lesion results separated the increase-driving route from the decrease-driving route, although both reach the same oscillator. The chirp-controlling PPn-C remained a separate premotor subdivision, so its role in chirps sits apart from both JAR routes. The target-cell assignments were later tested directly in intracellular recordings. Some of those assignments remained inferred in 1993. This was tested in the same circuit.

The vehicle injections served as the reference for every drug injection. Those controls separated chemical action from the injection itself. The control was run in parallel.

The vehicle control was essential because fluid injection into a small nucleus can alter the recording or local tissue apart from any receptor blockade. The artificial cerebrospinal fluid control isolates the drug's chemical action from the mechanical act of injecting. Injection into the pacemaker nucleus targeted the medullary cells that generate the oscillator's frequency changes. The antagonist response was measured against control injections in the same fish, and each animal served before and after drug delivery. Injecting into the pacemaker tested a step downstream of the upstream structures. Each animal's before and after records were compared directly.

2: **Eigenmannia virescens** is a South American weakly electric fish whose **electric organ discharge**, or EOD, repeats continuously. Heiligenberg described individual discharge frequencies between 300 and 600 Hz. The caudal electric organ generates the electric field that the fish uses to detect nearby objects in its environment. It is monitored continuously.

A neighboring fish with a similar frequency creates **interference** in the shared field. In the **jamming avoidance response**, or JAR, the focal fish shifts its discharge away from the neighbor's frequency. A lower-frequency neighbor elicits an increase, and a higher-frequency neighbor elicits a decrease. Removing the signal permits a return.

Published simultaneous recordings pair a 500-Hz EOD with one pacemaker command per cycle. The **pacemaker nucleus**, a hindbrain group that generates rhythmic commands, changes signal frequency rather than switching off the electric sense. Discharge frequency therefore serves as a measurable motor output. This output is measurable in every recorded cycle.
3: A **beat** is the slow modulation produced when two signals of similar frequency combine. **Amplitude** is the magnitude of a signal, and **phase** is the position within a repeating cycle. Heiligenberg represented the fish's discharge as S1 and the foreign signal as S2, and measured the mixed signal. Both sources contribute.

The mixed signal repeatedly grows and shrinks while its timing advances and delays relative to S1. These changes occur at the difference between the two source frequencies. A fast carrier can therefore hold a slow interference pattern that overlaps the amplitude changes used for object sensing. This is a slow envelope.

The original oscilloscope record preserves this relationship. **A beat rate alone** gives the size of a frequency difference, but it provides no information about whether the neighbor lies above or below the fish's own frequency. A fish that needs to choose a direction must use timing information from the mixture.
4: **Difference frequency**, written Δf, is the neighbor's frequency minus the fish's own frequency. Positive Δf requires the fish to lower its EOD, while negative Δf requires an increase. The sensory problem is therefore a decision about **sign**, not merely the detection of interference. The sign, not the size, determines the response.

Carr and colleagues depicted how an internal EOD source and an external, transverse source combine at the skin. Their example uses a 500-Hz EOD with neighbors at 495 or 505 Hz. Both neighbors produce 5-Hz amplitude beats, yet the relationship between amplitude change and timing reverses. Both cases differ in timing.

**Natural current geometry** supports this discrimination. The external source affects opposite body regions differently, while the internal discharge has a common origin. Paired amplitude and timing cues carry sign information, and the beat rate alone stays ambiguous. The neighbor's direction is encoded in the spatial pattern of the two cues.
5: An **amplitude ratio** compares the local strength of the foreign signal with the EOD substitute at one patch of skin. Heiligenberg analyzed two body regions with ratios of 0.3 and 0.1. The more contaminated region undergoes larger changes in both amplitude and phase during the same interference cycle. This is local.
